title: Does Hair of the Dog Work? Why Morning Drinking Backfires
excerpt: Does another drink really cure a hangover? Why hair of the dog feels like it works, what the methanol theory does and doesn't show, and why a morning beer usually makes things worse.
metaDescription: Does hair of the dog work? Why a morning drink eases a hangover briefly, what the methanol theory really shows, and why it usually backfires.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** hair of the dog (having another drink the morning after) can make you feel a bit better for an hour or two, but it doesn't cure a hangover. It postpones it. The most likely reason it seems to work is simple: a hangover kicks in as your blood alcohol falls back toward zero, and drinking again pushes that point later in the day. There's also an older, interesting idea about methanol that some people cite, but it's a hypothesis, not a proven fact. Meanwhile, the downsides are real: more alcohol for your liver to clear, worse sleep, a later and often rougher crash, and a habit that doctors treat as a warning sign of problem drinking.

**The quick rules:** Don't use a morning drink as a hangover remedy. If you've already had one, stop there, drink water, eat something, and give your body time. If you *need* a drink in the morning to stop shakiness, sweating, anxiety, or nausea, that's not a hangover trick, it may be alcohol withdrawal, and it's worth talking to a doctor about.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research on hangovers and morning drinking. It is not a substitute for advice from a doctor who knows your health history. **See a doctor or seek urgent care if** you get shaking hands, heavy sweating, a racing heart, confusion, or hallucinations when you stop drinking, if you've ever had a seizure after stopping alcohol, or if you regularly drink in the morning to feel normal. Stopping suddenly after long-term heavy drinking can be dangerous and should be done with medical support. In an emergency, call 911. In the US, the SAMHSA National Helpline (1-800-662-4357) is free, confidential, and open 24/7.

## What "Hair of the Dog" Actually Means

The phrase is a shortened form of "the hair of the dog that bit you." It comes from an old folk remedy: if a dog bit you, you were supposed to put some of that dog's hair on the wound. The idea that "like cures like" was later borrowed for drinking, so the cure for too much alcohol became a little more alcohol.

Today it usually means one of these:

- A beer with breakfast or brunch the day after a big night
- A Bloody Mary or mimosa at a late-morning brunch
- A "reviver" cocktail or a shot to "take the edge off"

The common thread is drinking alcohol specifically to make hangover symptoms go away. That's the practice this page looks at. A drink at brunch for its own sake is a separate question, though the same biology applies.

## Why It Seems to Work: The Withdrawal Postponement Explanation

The most widely accepted explanation is also the least exciting one. A hangover isn't really caused by the alcohol in your blood. It's what happens when the alcohol *leaves*.

Researchers who study hangovers define the hangover as the unpleasant mental and physical symptoms that show up after a single episode of drinking, **once blood alcohol concentration has returned to about zero**. That definition comes from consensus work by the Alcohol Hangover Research Group, a group of scientists who study the topic. The timing matters. Your worst symptoms tend to peak around the time your body finishes clearing the alcohol, often the morning after.

### What happens in your brain as the alcohol wears off

Alcohol has a calming, sedating effect on the brain. Very roughly, it boosts the activity of the brain's main "slow down" signal (a chemical messenger called GABA) and dampens its main "speed up" signal (glutamate). Over an evening of drinking, your brain adjusts to that pressure to keep things balanced.

When the alcohol is gone, that adjustment is still in place for a while, and the brain swings the other way. You end up in a mildly over-excited state. That's a big part of why a hangover can come with:

- Feeling jittery, anxious, or on edge (sometimes called "hangxiety")
- Sensitivity to light and noise
- A racing or pounding heart
- Shaky hands
- Restless, broken sleep in the early hours

If those symptoms sound like a very mild version of alcohol withdrawal, that's because many researchers think they overlap. The idea that a hangover is partly a "mini-withdrawal" is debated, and it doesn't explain everything about a hangover, but it fits these particular symptoms well.

### Why another drink "fixes" it

Put the pieces together and hair of the dog makes sense in a short-term way. If symptoms appear as alcohol falls toward zero, then drinking again pushes your blood alcohol back up. The calming effect returns, the jittery over-excitement eases, and you feel better.

Nothing has been repaired. You've just moved the finish line. Your body still has to clear all of the alcohol, including the new drink, and the hangover is waiting at the other end. Many people who try this find the second crash in the afternoon or evening is worse, not better, because there's now more alcohol to process and less sleep to recover with.

Alcohol also numbs pain and lifts mood a little for a while. On a morning when you have a headache and feel low, that's going to feel like relief. Relief and recovery are different things.

## The Methanol Idea: An Interesting Hypothesis, Not a Proven Fact

You'll often see a more scientific-sounding reason for hair of the dog, involving methanol. It's worth understanding, but it's important to be clear about how strong the evidence is. It's a hypothesis that hasn't been confirmed.

### Where methanol comes in

Most alcoholic drinks contain small amounts of **methanol** alongside the ethanol (the alcohol you're meant to drink). Methanol is one of the "congeners," the by-products of fermentation and aging that give drinks their flavor and color. Darker drinks such as brandy, whiskey, and red wine tend to have more congeners than clear drinks like vodka or gin. (For more on these compounds, see our guide to [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol).)

Your body breaks down both ethanol and methanol using the same liver enzyme, called alcohol dehydrogenase. Here's the key point: the enzyme strongly prefers ethanol. While there's ethanol around, methanol mostly waits its turn. Once the ethanol is gone, the enzyme gets to work on the methanol, turning it into formaldehyde and then formic acid. In large amounts, those are toxic. This is exactly why doctors have long used ethanol (and now a drug called fomepizole) as an antidote in methanol poisoning: keeping the enzyme busy stops methanol from being converted into its harmful products.

### How that's supposed to explain hair of the dog

The hypothesis goes like this. In the morning, your ethanol is gone and your body has started converting the leftover methanol. If those by-products contribute to hangover symptoms, then drinking more ethanol would keep the enzyme busy again and slow that conversion, which might ease symptoms for a while.

There is some research behind the first half of this. In the 1980s and 1990s, Swedish researchers including forensic toxicologist A.W. Jones measured methanol in people during the hangover phase and found that methanol stayed in the blood longer than ethanol, and that its clearance lined up with the timing of hangover symptoms. Studies comparing drinks also suggest higher-congener drinks can produce somewhat worse hangovers. A well-known US study published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2010 compared bourbon with vodka at the same alcohol dose and found people rated their hangovers as somewhat worse after bourbon.

### Why it's still just a hypothesis

There are good reasons not to treat the methanol story as settled:

- **The amounts are small.** The methanol in ordinary drinks is far below the levels seen in true methanol poisoning. Whether its breakdown products at these levels cause meaningful symptoms isn't proven.
- **Clear drinks still give bad hangovers.** Vodka has very little methanol, and people still get hangovers from it. In the bourbon-versus-vodka study, the difference between drinks was modest compared with the effect of the alcohol itself.
- **No good trials of hair of the dog exist.** As far as we know, nobody has run a controlled study showing that morning drinking reduces hangover symptoms through this pathway, rather than simply postponing withdrawal.

So the fair summary is this: the methanol idea is biologically plausible and has some supporting observations, but it's not established. Even if it's partly true, it would still mean hair of the dog only delays your body's clean-up. It doesn't remove the methanol. It just makes it wait longer.

## Why Hair of the Dog Backfires

Even setting the theory aside, there are practical reasons the morning drink tends to make things worse.

### 1. It adds to the alcohol your body has to clear

Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly steady pace, very roughly about one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot from person to person. There's no way to speed that up meaningfully. Every extra drink in the morning is more work for the same liver, which means more hours before you're truly back to zero, and more time spent in that low-grade hangover state.

### 2. It pushes the crash later, often to a worse time

A hangover at 9 a.m. on a Sunday is bad. A hangover that lands at 4 p.m. on Sunday, when you need to prepare for Monday, can be worse. Delaying symptoms often means they hit when you'd hoped to be over it. If you've ever had a hangover that seemed to drag on into a second day, a morning drink is one common cause. (See our article on the [two-day hangover](/never-hungover/two-day-hangover) for other reasons it happens.)

### 3. It makes dehydration and stomach irritation worse

Alcohol makes you urinate more by suppressing a hormone (vasopressin, also called antidiuretic hormone) that normally helps your kidneys hold on to water. It also irritates the stomach lining. A morning drink on an already upset stomach, often before you've eaten, adds to both problems. Dehydration isn't the whole story of a hangover, but it doesn't help with headache, thirst, or dizziness.

### 4. It wrecks the recovery sleep you need

Alcohol can help you fall asleep, but it disrupts sleep later in the night, especially REM sleep (the dreaming stage that matters for memory and mood). Poor sleep is a big reason people feel foggy and irritable the next day. Drinking in the morning or at midday can make that afternoon nap or the following night's sleep shallower and more broken. Our guide to [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025) covers how this works.

### 5. It's unsafe for driving and other tasks

People often underestimate how much alcohol is still in their system the morning after a heavy night. Adding a "small" morning drink on top of that can put you over legal driving limits or impair you at work, with tools, or while caring for children. If you'll need to drive, operate anything, or be fully alert, hair of the dog is a bad idea even before the hangover question.

### 6. It can turn into a pattern

This is the most important reason. Drinking in the morning to relieve the after-effects of drinking is one of the classic warning signs doctors look for. The CAGE questionnaire, a short screening tool for alcohol problems published in *JAMA* in 1984 by Dr. John Ewing and still widely used, includes exactly this question: have you ever had a drink first thing in the morning to steady your nerves or get rid of a hangover? (It calls this an "eye-opener.") The broader AUDIT screening tool, developed by the World Health Organization, asks a similar question.

That doesn't mean one mimosa at brunch makes someone an alcoholic. It means the habit of drinking *to fix the effects of drinking* is the same loop that keeps physical dependence going. Each round postpones withdrawal, and withdrawal gets harder to sit through.

## When It's Not a Hangover: Recognizing Withdrawal

For most people who drink occasionally, the morning after is a hangover and nothing more. But for people who drink heavily most days, the morning symptoms can be actual alcohol withdrawal, and that's a different situation.

Signs that it may be withdrawal rather than a normal hangover:

- You get shaky hands, sweating, anxiety, or nausea most mornings, not just after an unusually big night
- These symptoms ease quickly when you drink
- You've started planning to drink in the morning so you can function
- You feel worse each time you try to cut back

Alcohol withdrawal can be serious. In some people it progresses to severe agitation, hallucinations, seizures, or a dangerous condition called delirium tremens. **If this sounds like you, don't try to stop suddenly on your own.** Talk to a doctor. Medically supported withdrawal is safer and much more comfortable, and there are effective treatments. In the US, the SAMHSA National Helpline (1-800-662-4357) can point you to local help for free.

## "Does Drinking a Beer Help a Hangover?"

This is the most common version of the hair-of-the-dog question, so it deserves a direct answer.

A beer may make you feel a little better for a short while, for the reasons above: it nudges your blood alcohol back up, eases the jittery feeling, and has a mild pain-dulling effect. Beer also has a reputation as the "gentle" option because it's lower in alcohol per serving than spirits and contains water, some carbohydrate, and a little sodium and potassium.

But none of that makes it a hangover cure:

- **The water doesn't make up for the alcohol.** Beer still has a net drying effect because of the alcohol in it. A glass of water or an electrolyte drink does the hydration job better.
- **The carbohydrate is better from food.** Toast, crackers, eggs, or a banana will help steady your blood sugar and settle your stomach without adding alcohol.
- **It's still more alcohol to clear.** One beer is roughly one standard drink, which means roughly another hour or more of processing for your liver, and your hangover waits behind it.

What about non-alcoholic beer? It gives you the fluid, a few calories, and the familiar taste without adding alcohol. There's no strong evidence it treats a hangover, but it doesn't carry the same downsides. If the ritual of a cold beer helps you feel normal, an alcohol-free one is a reasonable swap.

## What About the Bloody Mary?

The Bloody Mary is the classic hair-of-the-dog drink, and people often argue it's the "healthy" choice because of the tomato juice. The tomato juice does bring fluid, some salt, and potassium, and the salty, savory taste can be easier on a queasy stomach.

The vodka cancels much of that out. If you like the drink, a "Virgin Mary" (tomato juice, lemon, Worcestershire sauce, hot sauce, celery salt, no vodka) gives you most of the benefits people are actually after: salt, fluid, and something with flavor. The same goes for mimosas: the orange juice can be useful, the sparkling wine is not.

## What Actually Helps a Hangover

There's no proven cure for a hangover. Time is the only thing that reliably ends one. But you can make the hours more bearable without adding alcohol:

- **Drink water or an electrolyte drink.** Sip steadily rather than gulping, especially if your stomach is upset.
- **Eat something simple.** Bland carbohydrates (toast, crackers, rice) and some protein (eggs) help with low energy and nausea.
- **Rest.** If you can, nap. Your brain is recovering from a night of disrupted sleep.
- **Consider a pain reliever carefully.** Ibuprofen or similar drugs can help a headache, but take them with food because alcohol and these drugs both irritate the stomach. Be cautious with acetaminophen (Tylenol) after heavy drinking. Our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains why, and when to ask a pharmacist first.
- **Light movement and fresh air.** A short walk won't "sweat out" alcohol, but many people feel clearer for it.
- **Coffee, in moderation.** It can help a caffeine-withdrawal headache if you usually drink it, but it doesn't speed up alcohol clearance.

For more detail on what the evidence supports, see our [science-based guide to curing a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-cure-a-hangover-complete-science-guide). If you're wondering how long you'll feel this way, our guide on [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last) covers typical timelines and what stretches them out. For how other well-known remedies hold up, from prairie oysters to celebrity breakfasts, see our check of [famous hangover cures](/never-hungover/famous-hangover-cures).

## Preventing the Next One Is More Useful Than Treating This One

The best way to avoid needing a cure is to drink in a way that makes a bad hangover less likely. The basics are well supported:

- **Drink less, or pace yourself.** The amount of alcohol is the biggest single factor in how bad a hangover is. Spacing drinks out gives your body more time to keep up.
- **Eat before and while drinking.** Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol is absorbed.
- **Alternate with water.** It slows your pace and keeps you hydrated.
- **Choose lighter drinks.** Clear spirits and lighter drinks tend to have fewer congeners than dark spirits and red wine. Our ranking of the [least hangover-causing alcohol](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked) goes into this.
- **Protect your sleep.** Stop drinking a few hours before bed if you can.

The order you drink things in matters less than people think, despite the old rhyme. The [beer before liquor](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth) saying is another myth worth checking.

Some people also take DHM (dihydromyricetin), a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, before or while drinking. Animal research suggests it may affect how the brain responds to alcohol and support alcohol metabolism, but human evidence is still limited and it is not a substitute for drinking less. If you're curious, our full guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers DHM alongside the habits that matter most, and what to realistically expect. If you'd like to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

Hair of the dog works the way borrowing money works: you feel better now and pay more later. The most likely reason a morning drink brings relief is that it lifts your blood alcohol back up and postpones the mild withdrawal-like state that makes up much of a hangover. The methanol explanation is an interesting hypothesis with some supporting research, but it isn't proven, and even if true it only delays your body's clean-up.

Meanwhile, the morning drink adds to dehydration, disrupts recovery sleep, can leave you impaired longer than you expect, and builds the exact habit doctors screen for when they look for alcohol problems. Water, food, rest, and time remain the honest answer. And if you find you need a drink in the morning to feel steady, that's a sign to talk to a doctor, not to reach for another drink.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does hair of the dog actually work?**

It can make you feel better for a short time, but it doesn't cure a hangover. Hangover symptoms tend to peak as your blood alcohol returns to zero. Drinking again raises it, which eases symptoms temporarily and postpones the hangover until the new alcohol is cleared too. Most people end up with a later, and often longer, recovery.

**Does drinking a beer help a hangover?**

A beer may take the edge off for an hour or so, but it adds more alcohol for your liver to process and delays recovery. The fluid in beer doesn't make up for the drying effect of the alcohol. Water or an electrolyte drink plus some simple food will do more good. A non-alcoholic beer is a reasonable swap if you want the ritual without the alcohol.

**Why does hair of the dog make you feel better?**

The leading explanation is that much of a hangover resembles mild alcohol withdrawal: the brain is over-excited after a night of being sedated by alcohol. Another drink brings back the sedating effect, so jitteriness, anxiety, and some aches ease. A second idea, that ethanol slows the breakdown of methanol into toxic by-products, is a hypothesis that hasn't been proven.

**Is the methanol theory of hangovers true?**

It's unproven. Ethanol does slow methanol breakdown, which is why it has been used as an antidote for methanol poisoning, and some studies found methanol lingers in the blood during the hangover phase. But the amounts in normal drinks are small, and people still get hangovers from low-methanol drinks like vodka. It may play a part, but it isn't established as a main cause of hangovers.

**Is drinking in the morning a sign of alcoholism?**

Not from one brunch drink. But regularly drinking in the morning to steady your nerves or relieve a hangover is a recognized warning sign. It appears as the "eye-opener" question in the CAGE screening questionnaire used by doctors. If you often need a morning drink to feel normal, talk to a doctor. Stopping suddenly after long-term heavy drinking can be dangerous without medical support.

**Is a Bloody Mary good for a hangover?**

The tomato juice, salt, and fluid can help a little, but the vodka works against them. A Virgin Mary (the same drink without alcohol) gives you the useful parts without adding more alcohol for your liver to clear.

**What should I do instead of hair of the dog?**

Drink water or an electrolyte drink, eat simple food, rest, and give your body time. A pain reliever such as ibuprofen taken with food can help a headache, but be cautious with acetaminophen (Tylenol) after heavy drinking. Time is the only thing that reliably ends a hangover.

**How long does a hangover last if you don't drink more?**

Most hangovers ease within about a day, often improving through the afternoon after a heavy night. They can last longer after very heavy drinking, poor sleep, or if you start drinking again. A morning drink is one of the more common reasons a hangover drags on.
